items.q: A 22-year-old motorcyclist sustains a high-energy traction injury to the right brachial plexus resulting in complete anesthesia in the C5 and C6 dermatomes and paralysis of shoulder abduction. Nerve conduction studies demonstrate an absent motor response in the axillary nerve but a completely preserved sensory nerve action potential (SNAP) of the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve. What is the anatomical level of this nerve lesion?
o: Preganglionic nerve root avulsion proximal to the dorsal root ganglion
Infraclavicular brachial plexus cord division injury
Isolated peripheral neurotmesis of the axillary nerve
items.e: In preganglionic root avulsion, the injury is proximal to the dorsal root ganglion (DRG), leaving the cell bodies in the DRG and their peripheral sensory axons intact. Because the distal sensory axon does not undergo Wallerian degeneration, sensory nerve action potentials (SNAPs) remain preserved despite complete clinical anesthesia in the corresponding dermatome.
items.note: Accurate, standard SS exam question on differentiating preganglionic from postganglionic plexus injuries via NCS.
items.reason: repeats fai20261122_046 (preganglionic avulsion with preserved SNAP)

items.q: Pathogens such as rabies virus, herpes simplex, and poliovirus, as well as neurotrophic signals like nerve growth factor (NGF) and tetanus toxin, travel from the axon terminal back to the neuronal cell body via which transport mechanism and motor protein?
o: Saltatory transport using sodium channel currents
items.e: Retrograde axonal transport moves vesicles, trophic signals (such as NGF), and specific neurotropic viruses and toxins from the peripheral axon terminal to the cell body using the motor protein dynein. Fast anterograde transport uses kinesin to move neurotransmitters and membrane vesicles away from the cell body.
items.note: Factually correct, clinically relevant basic science question directly matched to standard textbook details.

items.q: During local anaesthetic administration for peripheral nerve blockade, nerve fibres are blocked in a characteristic sequence based on axonal diameter and myelination. Which of the following nerve fibre types is blocked LAST by local anaesthetics?
items.e: Local anaesthetics block small, thinly myelinated or unmyelinated fibres first and large, heavily myelinated fibres last. The sequence of blockade sensitivity is B (autonomic) > A-delta and C (pain, temperature) > A-beta (touch, pressure) > A-alpha (motor and proprioception), meaning A-alpha fibres are blocked last and recover first.
items.note: High-yield standard question on Erlanger-Gasser nerve fibre classification and local anaesthetic susceptibility.

items.q: A 28-year-old man undergoes an Oberlin nerve transfer to restore elbow flexion following a proximal brachial plexus avulsion injury. Which donor nerve component is harvested to reinnervate the motor branch of the biceps muscle?
o: A motor fascicle of the ulnar nerve destined for the flexor carpi ulnaris
The entire main trunk of the median nerve
The anterior interosseous nerve branch supplying pronator quadratus
A motor fascicle of the radial nerve supplying the long head of triceps
items.e: The classic Oberlin nerve transfer uses a redundant motor fascicle of the ulnar nerve (specifically one supplying the flexor carpi ulnaris) transferred directly end-to-end to the biceps motor branch of the musculocutaneous nerve to restore active elbow flexion.
items.note: Clear, single-best answer question on a classic upper limb nerve transfer technique.

items.q: An orthopaedic surgeon evaluates a patient with a closed nerve injury 4 weeks after trauma. Electromyography (EMG) is performed to assess for axonal degeneration. How long after an acute nerve injury do spontaneous fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves typically first appear at rest on EMG in denervated skeletal muscle?
items.e: Spontaneous fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves indicate active axonal denervation of muscle and typically appear 2 to 3 weeks (10 to 21 days) following nerve injury. Electromyography is usually delayed until 3 to 4 weeks post-injury to accurately distinguish neurapraxia from axonal disruption.
items.note: Factually precise timing question routinely tested in superspeciality entrance examinations.

items.q: According to the sliding filament theory of skeletal muscle contraction, which band or zone of the sarcomere maintains a CONSTANT length during active cross-bridge cycling and shortening?
items.e: The A band corresponds to the total length of the thick myosin filaments and remains constant in length during muscle contraction. As actin filaments slide over myosin toward the M line, the I band and H zone shorten and the Z lines move closer together.
items.note: Basic muscle physiology question with unambiguous options and explanation.

items.q: During general anaesthesia for open reduction and internal fixation, a patient with underlying central core disease develops muscular rigidity, rapid hypercapnia (rising end-tidal CO2), and a severe temperature spike following succinylcholine administration. This acute reaction is caused by a genetic mutation affecting which sarcoplasmic reticulum structure?
items.e: Malignant hyperthermia is an autosomal dominant pharmacogenetic disorder linked to mutations in the ryanodine receptor 1 (RYR1) gene on the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Exposure to volatile anaesthetics or succinylcholine triggers uncontrolled calcium release into the sarcoplasm, leading to hypermetabolism, rigidity, hypercapnia, and hyperthermia; it is managed urgently with dantrolene.
items.note: Accurate high-yield topic bridging basic science, genetics, and clinical orthopaedic anaesthesia risks.

items.q: A track athlete presents with an acute tear of the biceps femoris long head at the myotendinous junction sustained during terminal swing phase while sprinting. Which type of muscle contraction generates the HIGHEST peak force and carries the greatest risk of structural muscle strain injury?
items.e: Eccentric contractions (where the muscle actively lengthens under load) produce the highest total force across the muscle unit, making them the primary cause of acute muscle strains and delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS), particularly at the myotendinous junction of two-joint muscles.
items.note: Classic muscle biomechanics and injury mechanisms question standard in post-graduate orthopaedic exams.

items.q: A surgeon evaluates a new serum biomarker for diagnosing prosthetic joint infection (PJI). When applying this test in a high-prevalence tertiary revision centre compared to a low-prevalence primary joint registry population, which of the following diagnostic parameters will increase?
items.e: Positive predictive value (PPV) depends directly on disease prevalence; as prevalence increases, PPV rises while negative predictive value (NPV) falls. Sensitivity, specificity, and likelihood ratios are intrinsic properties of the test and remain unchanged by disease prevalence.
items.note: Accurate, exam-worthy question directly testing the effect of prevalence on diagnostic test statistics.

items.q: An orthopaedic researcher aims to investigate potential risk factors for an extremely rare postoperative complication (incidence < 0.01%) following total ankle arthroplasty. Which study design is most appropriate and efficient for this objective?
items.e: Case-control studies start with the outcome (cases vs controls) and look backward for prior exposures, making them the most efficient design for studying rare diseases or rare outcomes. Prospective cohort studies and RCTs are inefficient for rare events because they would require unfeasibly large sample sizes.
items.note: Standard epidemiology question testing appropriate study design choice for rare outcomes.

items.q: During recruitment for a multicentre surgical trial, investigators use a central web-based randomisation service so that the enrolling clinician cannot foresee the upcoming treatment assignment. This procedure specifically ensures allocation concealment to prevent which type of bias?
items.e: Allocation concealment prevents enrolling clinicians from knowing or predicting the next treatment assignment, thereby preventing selection bias. Detection bias is prevented by blinded outcome assessment, performance bias by blinding care providers/patients, and attrition bias by maintaining high follow-up and intention-to-treat analysis.
items.note: Classic distinction between allocation concealment (selection bias) and blinding (performance/detection bias).

items.q: A clinical trial compares non-normally distributed Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) pain scores recorded at 6 weeks postoperatively between two independent treatment groups of 20 patients each. Which statistical test is most appropriate for comparing these two groups?
items.e: The Mann-Whitney U test (Wilcoxon rank-sum test) is the non-parametric statistical test used to compare non-normally distributed continuous or ordinal data between two independent groups. Paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests are reserved for paired or repeated measures within the same subjects.
items.note: Standard statistical test selection rule for non-normally distributed independent continuous/ordinal data.

items.q: In a randomised trial evaluating a new antibiotic-impregnated bone cement for open tibia fractures, the deep infection rate is 15% in the standard control group and 5% in the experimental treatment group. What is the Number Needed to Treat (NNT) to prevent one deep infection?
items.e: The Absolute Risk Reduction (ARR) is the Control Event Rate minus the Experimental Event Rate (15% - 5% = 10% or 0.10). The Number Needed to Treat (NNT) is calculated as 1 / ARR (1 / 0.10 = 10).
items.note: Fully accurate calculation of NNT from ARR.

items.q: When calculating long-term implant survivorship of a total hip prosthesis in an elderly population, using standard Kaplan-Meier survival analysis in the presence of death as a competing risk leads to which of the following statistical errors?
o: Underestimation of the cumulative revision rate
Overestimation of the cumulative revision rate
Falsely low hazard ratio in Cox regression
items.e: Kaplan-Meier survival analysis censors subjects who die before revision, assuming they remain at risk of revision. In elderly cohorts where death is a major competing risk, Kaplan-Meier overestimates the cumulative revision rate; a cumulative incidence function (Fine and Gray method) should be used instead.
items.note: Important statistical concept in registry and joint replacement survivorship literature.

items.q: Two orthopaedic surgeons independently grade 50 proximal humerus fractures using the Neer classification system. Which statistical metric is most appropriate for evaluating inter-observer reliability for this categorical classification?
items.e: Cohen's kappa coefficient measures agreement between two observers for categorical data while correcting for agreement occurring by chance alone. The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) is used to assess reliability for continuous quantitative variables.
items.note: High-yield statistical concept regarding observer agreement and reliability metrics.

items.q: An orthopaedic researcher is preparing a manuscript reporting a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials comparing hemiarthroplasty with total hip arthroplasty for displaced femoral neck fractures. Which reporting guideline checklist must be followed?
items.e: PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) is the mandatory reporting guideline checklist and flow diagram for systematic reviews and meta-analyses. CONSORT is used for randomised controlled trials, STROBE for observational studies, and STARD for diagnostic accuracy studies.
items.note: Standard question on EQUATOR network study reporting guidelines.

items.q: A surgical team is performing a fluoroscopy-guided femoral intramedullary nailing. To minimize radiation scatter and staff exposure, how should the C-arm be configured, and where should the operating surgeon stand during a lateral view?
o: X-ray tube above the table, image intensifier below; surgeon stands on the tube side
X-ray tube below the table, image intensifier close to the patient on top; surgeon stands on the image intensifier side
X-ray tube below the table, image intensifier placed far above the patient; surgeon stands on the tube side
X-ray tube above the table, image intensifier close to the patient below; surgeon stands on the image intensifier side
items.e: Scatter radiation is greatest on the entrance/X-ray tube side of the patient. Placing the tube under the table and the image intensifier close to the patient on top reduces patient entrance dose and scatter, while standing on the image intensifier side during lateral views minimizes occupational scatter exposure to the surgeon.
items.note: Accurate, exam-worthy question directly aligned with ICRP guidelines and standard surgical orthopaedic safety principles.
items.reason: repeats existing C-arm scatter positioning questions

items.q: A 35-year-old athlete undergoes shoulder MRI. Increased signal intensity is observed near the supraspinatus insertion on T1-weighted and proton density sequences, but the area appears completely normal with low signal intensity on T2-weighted sequences. What physical phenomenon explains this finding?
items.e: The magic angle effect occurs when collagen fibres (such as in the supraspinatus tendon) are oriented at approximately 55 degrees to the main magnetic field (B0). This causes falsely increased signal on short-TE sequences (T1, PD, GRE), mimicking tendinopathy or a tear, but the elevated signal disappears on long-TE sequences like T2.
items.note: Classic MRI physics artefact question frequently tested in orthopaedic superspeciality exams.

items.q: According to the ICRP guidelines for radiation protection, what is the annual effective dose limit for an occupational radiation worker (averaged over 5 years) and the specific annual limit for the lens of the eye?
o: 20 mSv per year (effective dose) and 20 mSv per year (lens of the eye)
50 mSv per year (effective dose) and 150 mSv per year (lens of the eye)
20 mSv per year (effective dose) and 500 mSv per year (lens of the eye)
1 mSv per year (effective dose) and 20 mSv per year (lens of the eye)
items.e: ICRP recommendations set the occupational limit for annual effective dose to 20 mSv per year averaged over 5 years (not exceeding 50 mSv in any single year). The dose limit for the lens of the eye was lowered in 2011 to 20 mSv per year averaged over 5 years to reduce the risk of radiation-induced cataracts.
items.note: Factually correct dose limits matching updated ICRP standard recommendations.

items.q: During CT evaluation of a complex intra-articular fracture, attenuation values are measured in Hounsfield Units (HU). Which of the following tissue/material pairs is correctly matched with its typical HU value?
o: Fat: -100 to -50 HU; Cortical bone: +1000 HU or more
items.e: On the Hounsfield scale, water is defined as 0 HU and air is -1000 HU. Fat has negative values (-100 to -50 HU), whereas cortical bone has high attenuation (+1000 HU or more); cancellous bone typically ranges between +300 and +700 HU.
items.note: Factually flawless question covering fundamental CT attenuation scales.

items.q: A 62-year-old postmenopausal woman undergoes DEXA scanning. Her T-score at the femoral neck is -2.8, and she has no prior history of low-energy fractures. According to the WHO criteria, how should her bone density be categorized?
items.e: According to WHO criteria based on T-scores in postmenopausal women, a score of -1.0 or higher is normal, between -1.0 and -2.5 is osteopenia, and -2.5 or lower defines osteoporosis. Severe (established) osteoporosis requires a T-score of -2.5 or lower combined with one or more fragility fractures.
items.note: Standard WHO diagnostic criteria question for osteoporosis.

items.q: During a musculoskeletal ultrasound examination of the patellar tendon, a dark, hypoechoic area is observed. Tipping the transducer slightly (heel-toe maneuver) so that the sound beam meets the tendon fibres at a 90-degree angle restores normal hyperechoic fibrillar architecture. What artefact was present initially?
items.e: Anisotropy occurs when an ultrasound beam strikes ordered fibrillar structures (like tendons or ligaments) at a non-perpendicular angle, causing sound waves to reflect away from the transducer and creating a false hypoechoic appearance. Angling the probe perpendicular to the fibres resolves the artefact.
items.note: High-yield ultrasound physics phenomenon in orthopaedic imaging.

items.q: A Technetium-99m MDP bone scan is ordered for a patient with back pain. Which of the following conditions characteristically produces a photopenic ("cold") lesion on a radionuclide bone scan?
items.e: Multiple myeloma characteristically presents as photopenic or cold lesions on Technetium-99m bone scans because it causes purely osteolytic destruction without stimulating an osteoblastic repair response. Osteoid osteoma, Paget disease, and healing fractures all demonstrate increased (hot) osteoblastic radionuclide uptake.
items.note: Standard nuclear medicine fact commonly tested in musculoskeletal radiology modules.

items.q: Which statement accurately describes X-ray interactions with human tissue during clinical orthopaedic radiography?
o: Compton scatter probability is directly proportional to atomic number cubed (Z cubed)
Photoelectric absorption is dominant in bone at lower photon energies and is responsible for image contrast
The photoelectric effect is the main source of occupational scatter radiation dose to operating theatre personnel
Compton scatter occurs when an incident photon is completely absorbed by an inner-shell electron
items.e: The photoelectric effect involves complete absorption of photons by inner-shell electrons and is proportional to Z cubed / E cubed, making it dominant at lower energies in high-atomic-number materials like bone (calcium), which creates radiographic image contrast. Compton scatter involves outer-shell electron interactions and is the main source of occupational scatter dose to operating room staff.
items.note: Core radiophysics question distinguishing photoelectric and Compton interactions accurately.

items.q: A 68-year-old female is prescribed annual intravenous zoledronic acid following surgical fixation of a fragility hip fracture. What is the specific cellular enzymatic mechanism by which nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates induce osteoclast dysfunction and apoptosis?
o: Competitive inhibition of carbonic anhydrase II
Direct inhibition of farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway
Antagonism of the receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand (RANKL)
Formation of toxic ATP analogues within the osteoclast cytoplasm
items.e: Nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates (such as zoledronate and alendronate) inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway, preventing protein prenylation and causing osteoclast dysfunction and apoptosis. Non-nitrogen bisphosphonates form toxic ATP analogues, while denosumab targets RANKL.
items.note: Accurate, clear single-best answer question fully supported by text notes.

items.q: During a total knee arthroplasty performed under nerve blocks, a patient suddenly develops perioral tingling, tinnitus, a metallic taste, followed by generalised tonic-clonic seizures. What is the recommended lipid resuscitation protocol for local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST)?
o: 20% lipid emulsion: 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus followed by an infusion of 0.25 mL/kg/min
10% lipid emulsion: 3.0 mL/kg IV bolus followed by an infusion of 0.5 mL/kg/min
20% lipid emulsion: 5.0 mL/kg IV bolus followed by an infusion of 1.0 mL/kg/min
10% lipid emulsion: 0.5 mL/kg IV bolus followed by an infusion of 0.1 mL/kg/min
items.e: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) presents with early CNS excitation (perioral tingling, metallic taste, tinnitus, seizures) followed by cardiovascular collapse. Management includes airway control and administration of 20% lipid emulsion as a 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus followed by an infusion at 0.25 mL/kg/min.
items.note: High-yield standard emergency protocol, precise values, unambiguous distractor options.

items.q: A 58-year-old female with severe rheumatoid arthritis is scheduled for elective primary total hip arthroplasty. She takes weekly oral methotrexate and subcutaneous adalimumab every 2 weeks. According to current ACR/AAHKS guidelines, how should these medications be managed perioperatively?
o: Stop methotrexate 2 weeks prior to surgery; withhold adalimumab so surgery is performed in the 3rd week after the last dose
Continue methotrexate without interruption; withhold adalimumab so surgery is performed in the 3rd week after the last dose
Continue both methotrexate and adalimumab through the perioperative period without interruption
Stop both methotrexate and adalimumab 4 weeks prior to surgery and restart on postoperative day 1
items.e: According to ACR/AAHKS guidelines, conventional DMARDs like methotrexate should be continued through elective arthroplasty. Biologics like adalimumab (dosed every 2 weeks) should be withheld and surgery scheduled at the end of the dosing cycle (i.e. in week 3 after the prior dose).
items.note: Tests key updated guideline consensus on perioperative DMARD management correctly.

items.q: During cementation of a femoral stem in an elderly patient undergoing hemiarthroplasty for a hip fracture, the patient develops severe intraoperative hypoxia with an SpO2 of 86% and a 45% fall in systolic blood pressure. According to the Donaldson classification, which grade of Bone Cement Implantation Syndrome (BCIS) is present?
items.e: Under the Donaldson classification for Bone Cement Implantation Syndrome (BCIS), Grade 1 involves moderate hypoxia (SpO2 < 94%) or a systolic BP fall > 20%. Grade 2 is defined by severe hypoxia (SpO2 < 88%), a systolic BP fall > 40%, or unexpected loss of consciousness. Grade 3 involves cardiovascular collapse requiring CPR.
items.note: Accurate application of the Donaldson BCIS classification.

items.q: Which of the following antimicrobial agents exerts its antibacterial effect by inhibiting bacterial RNA polymerase and is specifically used as adjunctive therapy in staphylococcal implant-associated orthopaedic infections due to its activity against biofilm?
items.e: Rifampicin acts by inhibiting bacterial RNA polymerase and possesses specific activity against staphylococcal biofilm in implant infections. It should never be used as monotherapy due to the rapid development of resistance.
items.note: Direct standard pharmacology question testing mechanism and orthopaedic relevance.

items.q: During spine surgery under general anaesthesia using volatile anaesthetics, the anaesthetist notes an unexplained, rapid rise in end-tidal CO2, followed by generalized muscle rigidity and masseter spasm. Which targeted therapeutic agent must be immediately administered?
o: Protamine sulfate 1 mg per 100 units IV
items.e: An unexplained rise in end-tidal CO2 is the earliest clinical sign of malignant hyperthermia (commonly caused by RYR1 mutations triggered by volatile anaesthetics or succinylcholine). Immediate management includes stopping triggers, hyperventilation, and IV dantrolene at 2.5 mg/kg, which blocks calcium release from the ryanodine receptor.
items.note: Classic subspecialty perioperative emergency management question.

items.q: A patient undergoing total hip arthroplasty has an epidural catheter placed for postoperative analgesia and is receiving prophylactic low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH). According to ASRA guidelines, what is the minimum required interval between the last prophylactic LMWH dose and epidural catheter removal?
items.e: ASRA guidelines specify that for prophylactic LMWH, at least 12 hours must elapse between the last dose and neuraxial needle insertion or epidural catheter removal (24 hours for therapeutic LMWH doses). The next dose should be given at least 4 hours after catheter removal.
items.note: Crucial safety guideline question regarding neuraxial anaesthesia and anticoagulation.

items.q: Romosozumab is a sclerostin-inhibiting monoclonal antibody that exerts a dual action of increasing bone formation and decreasing bone resorption. Which of the following clinical scenarios represents an absolute contraindication to initiating romosozumab?
o: History of myocardial infarction or stroke within the preceding year
Unexplained elevation of serum alkaline phosphatase
Presence of open physes or Paget disease of bone
Renal impairment with CrCl below 35 mL/min
items.e: Romosozumab was shown in the ARCH trial to carry an increased risk of serious cardiovascular events compared to alendronate. Therefore, it is contraindicated and should be avoided in patients who have suffered a myocardial infarction or stroke within the past year.
items.note: Tests critical drug contraindications for a recently approved anabolic osteoporosis agent.

items.q: A 28‑year‑old male presents with a vertical shear pelvic injury following a motor‑vehicle collision. CT shows a vertical displacement of the right hemipelvis with an ipsilateral L5 transverse process avulsion. Which of the following is most likely to be true about this fracture pattern?
o: The posterior sacroiliac ligaments are intact
The anterior sacroiliac ligaments are torn
The injury is marginally stable with a small (≤2 cm) symphyseal widening
items.e: Vertical shear (VS) fractures involve disruption of both the anterior and posterior sacroiliac ligaments and are characterized by a complete vertical displacement of the hemipelvis. L5 transverse process avulsion is a classic indicator of vertical instability.
items.note: Correct answer aligns with the definition of VS injuries; distractor A contradicts ligamental injury; distractor C mislabels instability; distractor D misstates symphyseal widening.

items.q: In an APC II pelvic fracture, the symphyseal opening is 3.2 cm. What is the preferred initial non‑operative intervention to prevent tamponade of venous bleeding in the acute phase?
o: Application of a pelvic binder over the greater trochanters
Preperitoneal pelvic packing without external fixation
items.e: A pelvic binder should be applied at the level of the greater trochanters, internally rotating and tying the legs. This reduces posterior pelvic volume and tamponades venous bleeding without over‑compressing the lateral wall in APC injuries.
items.note: Binder is standard immediate non‑operative management per guidelines; other choices are inappropriate or addressed later steps.

items.q: During a modified Stoppa approach for a bi‑column acetabular fracture, which vascular structure is most at risk of injury?
items.e: The corona mortis is an anastomosis between the external iliac or inferior epigastric and the obturator vessels, situated behind the superior pubic ramus, and is a well‑known danger during anterior intrapelvic approaches.
items.note: Coronary mortis is the classic risk; other options are either not present or less likely.

items.q: A 52‑year‑old man with a posterior wall acetabular fracture undergoes a Kocher‑Langenbeck approach. Which nerve is most vulnerable if the surgeon extends the hip beyond 0° and flexes the knee less than 90°?
items.e: The sciatic nerve lies adjacent to the posterior wall; keeping the hip extended and the knee flexed protects it. Excessive hip extension or insufficient knee flexion increases the risk of traction injury.
items.note: Sciatic nerve is the correct at‑risk structure; distractors are anatomically separated.

items.q: Which of the following is the definitive imaging modality for assessing rotational instability in a suspected pelvis ring injury?
items.e: CT with 3‑D reconstruction is the standard for evaluating sacral fractures, SI joint disruption and rotational mechanics, surpassing plain radiographs in detail.
items.note: CT is universally accepted as the gold standard for rotational instability; plain views are insufficient.

items.q: A 72‑year‑old woman falls from standing height and presents with anterior thigh pain. Plain AP pelvis radiograph is normal. Which imaging modality should be obtained first to rule out an occult femoral neck fracture?
items.e: MRI within hours of injury is the most sensitive and specific test for occult femoral neck fractures and can detect associated intra‑abdominal injuries; it is preferred over delayed radiographs, ultrasound or bone scan.
items.note: MRI is the gold standard for occult neck fractures.
items.reason: repeats b998 occult femoral neck MRI

items.q: A 27‑year‑old motorcyclist is admitted with a vertical Pauwels III femoral neck fracture and a concomitant vertical basicervical fracture. Which fixation device provides the best resistance to the vertical shear forces?
o: Sliding hip screw with an anti‑rotation screw
Dynamic hip screw with a medial buttress plate
items.e: A proximal femoral locking nail (PFNA) is a fixed‑angle construct that best resists high‑angle vertical shear in Pauwels III fractures, whereas the other options provide less shear resistance. The marked answer (medial buttress plate) is incorrect because a fixed‑angle nail is superior for this pattern.
items.note: PFNA gives fixed‑angle stability against vertical shear.

items.q: An 82‑year‑old bedridden patient with bilateral hip arthroplasty is found to have a displaced intertrochanteric fracture of the right femur with a thin (<20 mm) lateral wall on the last‑minute CT. According to current guidelines, which implant is most appropriate?
o: Dynamic hip screw (DHS) with a 135° screw
items.e: A thin lateral wall predicts failure of a DHS; a cephalomedullary nail is the implant of choice for unstable pertrochanteric fractures with a deficient lateral wall.
items.note: Cephalomedullary nails are the treatment of choice for unstable pertrochanteric fractures.

items.q:
A 65‑year‑old female has a comminuted, purely depressed lateral tibial plateau fracture (Schatzker III). Which of the following is the most important reason to consider urgent arthroplasty instead of ORIF?
A. Presence of a popliteal artery injury
B. The fracture‑blisters are healing with a wrinkle sign
C. The mechanical axis is not restored after reduction
D. Medial meniscal tear detected on MRI
items.e: In elderly patients with severe comminution (Schatzker III) and consequent inability to restore the mechanical axis, early total knee arthroplasty is preferred as it provides better alignment, reduces the risk of post‑traumatic arthritis, and bypasses the challenge of maintaining a stable construct.
items.note: Mechanical axis maintenance is the key factor in deciding arthroplasty.

items.q: A 24‑year‑old male presents with a supination‑external‑rotation ankle injury. Radiographs show a Weber B fibular fracture at the level of the syndesmosis and a comminuted medial malleolar fracture with medial clear space >5 mm on a weight‑bearing AP film. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
o: Closed reduction and casting with early weight bearing for 6 weeks
Immediate ORIF of the fibula and medial malleolus with a lateral plate and medial screws
External fixation of the syndesmosis followed by delayed fixation of the malleoli
items.e: The medial clear space is widened, indicating medial shift and a deltoid injury. In a Weber B fracture with medial instability, operative fixation of both malleoli is required to restore the mortise.
items.note: Question is clear, options are mutually exclusive and evidence-based.

items.q: A 50‑year‑old female sustains an isolated posterior malleolar fragment involving 30 % of the tibiotalar joint surface. What is the current threshold for direct fixation of this fragment according to contemporary evidence?
items.e: Studies now show that fragments covering 25–30 % of the joint surface destabilise the ankle and warrant fixation, even if they are displaced.
items.note: Evidence-based, single best answer.

items.q: During an AP ankle radiograph taken 1 cm above the plafond, the tibiofibular clear space measures 6.5 mm. Which of the following diagnoses is most likely?
items.e: A tibiofibular clear space >5‑6 mm is the most reliable radiographic sign of a syndesmotic injury.
items.note: Evidence-based, correct.

items.q: A 72‑year‑old woman presents with a displaced surgical‑neck fracture of the proximal humerus. Which factor would most strongly predict post‑fracture osteonecrosis of the humeral head?
o: Metaphyseal extension less than 8 mm attached to the head
items.e: Hertel’s criteria identify a metaphyseal extension < 8 mm under the head as a key predictor of head ischaemia.
items.note: Fact directly taken from notes

items.q: During fixation of a two‑part surgical‑neck fracture in a young adult, the surgeon places a locking plate from the anterolateral aspect. Which technical point is most critical to avoid varus collapse?
o: Using screws that cross the articular surface
Fixing the plate as high as possible on the shaft
Including an inferomedial calcar screw for medial support
Drilling the screws at a 45° angle to the shaft
items.e: Medial calcar support is essential; loss of this leads to varus collapse and screw cut‑out.
items.note: Directly reflected in the notes.

items.q: A 25‑year‑old woman falls and sustains an anterior shoulder dislocation. On examination, she has a positive apprehension test and a laxation of the AC joint on the affected side. What is the most likely associated shoulder structure injury?
items.e: Anterior dislocations are classically associated with a Bankart (anteroinferior labral) lesion.
items.note: Standard complication of anterior dislocation.

items.q: A 45‑year‑old man presents with a displaced transverse olecranon fracture and a stable ulnohumeral joint. Which fixation method is most appropriate?
items.e: Tension‑band wiring converts triceps tension into compression across the articular surface and is the gold‑standard for transverse, non‑comminuted olecranon fractures.
items.note: Correct choice matches standard practice.

items.q: During surgery for a radial head fracture, the surgeon places screws in the *safe zone* to avoid impingement on the proximal radioulnar joint. In neutral forearm rotation, the safe zone lies:
o: Lateral between the radial styloid and Lister's tubercle
items.e: The safe zone is a 90‑degree non‑articular arc on the lateral aspect of the radial head in neutral rotation.
items.note: Matches classic description.

items.q: An elderly patient with a comminuted distal humerus fracture (AO 13C3) who is low demand and osteoporotic is best managed with:
o: Locked plating with a lateral plate only
items.e: In osteoporotic, irreconstructable C3 fractures, a total elbow arthroplasty provides early pain relief and functional restoration.
items.note: Standard treatment per Campbell.

items.q: In a radial head fracture (Mason type III) associated with a medial collateral ligament tear, the recommended treatment is:
items.e: The radial head must be preserved or replaced as a secondary stabiliser to valgus forces when the MCL is deficient.
items.note: Matches Campbell’s treatment algorithm.

items.q: A 55‑year‑old woman with a displaced Monteggia equivalent injury shows intact internal fixation of the ulna and a Grade 2 radial head fracture. The most likely joint instability is due to:
